1. Problem Statement
To design a positionally adaptable orthopedic device for growing children (ages 5-7) to
accommodate up to 10% volumetric foot growth while supporting 150N of ground
reaction forces.


2. Project Background Report

2.1 Disease State & Procedure Understanding
Disease Background

Pes planus, commonly referred to as flat feet, is a common foot deformity characterized
by partial or complete loss of the medical longitudinal arch during weight-bearing.

Consists of several flexible and rigid subtypes.




Figure 1. Typical Arch vs Flat Arch secondary Pes planus [3].

Causes:

Congenital:

Infants are commonly born with flat feet and do not develop a normal arch until ages 7 to
10. This is because infants have a pad of fat that lies under the medial longitudinal arch
that protects the arch during early childhood but rapidly disappears as the child starts
walking.

However, some children might just not develop a normal arch by the time they reach
adulthood.

Acquired:

Acquired pes planus is most commonly associated with posterior tibial tendon
dysfunction, which supports the arch and provides inversion and plantarflexion of the
foot.

Dysfunction of this tendon can result from stretching, tears, or ruptures.

Likewise, patients with damage or trauma to the midfoot or hindfoot that results in
navicular, first metatarsal, calcaneal, or Lisfranc ligament complex are at an increased
risk of developing pes planus.

Other causes consist of injuries to soft tissues such as the plantar fascia or spring
ligament.

Patients who exhibit congenital ligamentous laxity due to Down syndrome, Marfan
syndrome, or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome can also present with pes planus.

Patients with rheumatoid arthritis or other degenerative or inflammatory conditions are
likewise at higher risk of pes planus.

Symptoms:

Early symptoms might include foot pain, ankle pain, and shin splints.

Over time, patients tend to develop abnormalities in their gait, deformities like bunions or
hammertoes, and even constant chronic pain.

This pain can spread upstream to the knees, hips, and lower back as well.

If left untreated, many patients develop conditions secondary to pes planus, such as
arthritis, ankle instability and strains, and other repetitive strain-based injuries.

Current Treatment Methods:

Children rarely require surgical intervention for pes planus. Foot orthotics are often the
primary treatment for foot pain resulting from pes planus in children.

However, surgery may be suggested for more severe cases of rigid pes planus, tarsal
coalitions, and progressive, symptomatic pes planus.

Limitations of Current Treatments:

The majority of treatments for pes planus are limited because most cases are
asymptomatic and developmentally normal.

Research Summary:

Molina-García, C., Banwell, G., Rodríguez-Blanque, R., Sánchez-García, J. C., Reinoso-
Cobo, A., Cortés-Martín, J., & Ramos-Petersen, L. (2023). Efficacy of Plantar Orthoses
in Paediatric Flexible Flatfoot: A Five-Year Systematic Review. Children, 10(2), 371.
https://doi.org/10.3390/children10020371

Summary: This systematic review evaluates multiple clinical trials tracking pediatric
cohorts presenting with symptomatic flexible flatfoot. The article notes that orthotics
treatment is the most commonly recommended treatment amoung pediatrics despite

lack of supporting evidence for such treatment, along with a lack of evidence supporting
the effectiveness of orthotics for this matter, indicating the presence of bias in several of
the reviewed studies in testing and validation methods.

Sharula, Zhao F, Wu T, Kang Q, Geng X, Qin H, Zhang Y, He J, Huang L, Xu J and Lu S
(2026) Treatment of pediatric flatfoot: a systematic review-based consensus and
guidelines by CPAM-LRC. Front. Pediatr. 14:1825355. doi: 10.3389/fped.2026.1825355

Summary: This multi-disciplinary clinical guideline synthesizes database trials to outline
standard care pathways for pediatric flatfoot management. The expert panel notes that
the pediatric medial longitudinal arch develops progressively during the first decade of
life, meaning that conservative treatment must avoid completely rigid immobilization to
prevent secondary muscle atrophy. The text concludes that successful conservative
interventions require designs capable of accommodating dynamic developmental
changes while simultaneously mitigating the localized pain and functional limits that
trigger clinical consultations.

Dars, S., Uden, H., Banwell, H. A., & Kumar, S. (2018). The effectiveness of non-
surgical intervention (Foot Orthoses) for paediatric flexible pes planus: A systematic
review: Update. PloS one, 13(2), e0193060.
https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0193060

Summary: This systematic review addresses the clinical efficacy and wear compliance
profiles of foot orthoses across pediatric populations. Out of 606 articles identified, 11
studies met the inclusion criteria. A diverse range of pre-fabricated and customised FOs
were utilised and effectiveness measured through a plethora of outcomes. Summarised
findings from the heterogeneous evidence base indicated that FOs may have a positive
impact across a range of outcomes including pain, foot posture, gait, function and
structural and kinetic measures. Despite these consistent positive outcomes reported in
several studies, the current evidence base lacks clarity and uniformity in terms of
diagnostic criteria, interventions delivered, and outcomes measured for paediatric
flexible pes planus.

Procedural Flow Diagram (Generated per deliverables)
1. Diagnosis: Patient aged 5-7 presents to pediatrician or podiatrist with foot fatigue,
pain, or observed gait abnormalities.
2. Assessment: Clinical evaluation of Resting Calcaneal Stance Position (RCSP) and
Medial Longitudinal Arch (MLA) collapse under load.
3. Prescription/Treatment: Recommendation of non-surgical intervention (foot orthotics)
to alleviate pain while preserving dynamic arch growth.
4. Application: Parent applies orthotic device to the child's foot daily.
5. Failure Modes in Pathway: Child refuses to wear rigid orthotic due to pain/stiffness;
device limits natural arch muscle development; device is rapidly outgrown resulting in
improper fit.

2.2 Competitive Benchmark
User Analysis:

All users of this device will fall into the three P’s: Patients, Providers, and Payers.

Each of these groups all have different needs that will have to be factored into our
design, and we should keep all stakeholders in mind when making design decisions.

First, there are multiple people to consider when thinking about the patient's needs.

Since this device is targeted at children aged 5-7 with Pes Planus, it must be not only
comfortable for the child, but easy for the child’s parent to use and put on them.

Furthermore, the device must be very durable to survive daily use from a toddler.

Overall, the patients using this will be children aged 5-7 years at risk of developing Pes
Planus, and to accommodate them best we must make an easy to use yet durable
device that will improve the child's arch.

Next, there are a wide range of providers that may recommend this device.

A pediatric podiatrist may prescribe this device to the patient at a doctor's office, a
physical therapist may suggest it during a recovery session, and a general practitioner
may refer a family to one of these professionals if the problem is presented to them.

Ideally, the doctor will only need to demonstrate how to use the device to the family and
initially set it up for the child.

This once again means the device must be easy to use, since many different
professionals may be using it, and it must work so that the doctor continues to
recommend them to families.

Overall, the needs of the provider of the device are very similar to the needs of the
patient's device: to prevent flat feet from forming and to be simple to operate.

Lastly, the payers of the device will be insurance companies and hospitals, which want
the device to make profit and be safe enough to avoid any liability.

If the device poses a significant risk to the patient, such as inducing Pes Planus instead
of preventing it, the payers will be liable for the damages that are caused.

The main priority of the payers is to get a return on their investment, meaning the device
must work well enough to sell to patients, and it must prioritize safety while doing so.

Overall, the users may have different motives for their needs, however a safe, durable
device that successfully prevents Pes Planus will make everyone happy.

2.3 Conclusion (So What?)
As synthesized from the above research and competitive benchmarking, standard rigid
orthotics present substantial limitations for pediatric patients due to the rapid volumetric
foot growth between ages 5 to 7. Traditional interventions frequently fail due to low
compliance caused by physical discomfort and the high cost of constant replacement.
Group 11’s solution presents a strong commercial and clinical opportunity by offering a
positionally adaptable, comfortable sleeve-based design that scales with the child’s
growth. This reduces pain efficiently while lowering the financial burden on parents and
payers, fulfilling a critical unmet need in pediatric podiatry.

3.2 CFR 820.30 (c) Design and Development Inputs
Design User Needs & Decision Making – Group 11

Chosen Video: Best Plantar Fasciitis Arch Support Sleeves

The application of the arch support sleeve starts at 0:21 seconds in the video.

The gowning process simply includes stretching the sleeve, sliding the foot into the
sleeve, and positioning it around the arch of the foot.

Once the sleeve is properly placed, the patient can put on regular socks and shoes over
it and continue with their day.

Use Case Description:

This video provides instructions for the patient to apply the sleeve on themselves at their
own home.

This would likely be done in the home immediately after waking up, since it is
recommended for every-day, normal activity.

The gowning process for the sleeve is very simple and can fit seamlessly into a patient's
routine.

Task List:

Stretch the sleeve enough for your foot to fit through

Slide foot into the sleeve

Position the gel pad under arch of the foot

Let go of sleeve and ensure the pad is adequately compressed against the arch of the
foot.

Sub-Task Breakdown:

Stretch the sleeve enough for your foot to fit through

1.1. Place fingers inside the sleeve

1.2. Pull sleeve in opposite directions to create a larger opening

1.3. Ensure that the opening is large enough to fit around your foot

Slide foot into the sleeve

2.1. Place foot through stretched sleeve

2.2. Pull sleeve towards yourself until it is fully wrapped around your foot

Position the gel pad under arch of the foot

3.1. Feel the bottom of your foot to locate your arch

3.2. Feel the bottom of the sleeve to locate the arch support

3.3. Pull the sleeve up or down your foot until the pad fits comfortably in your arch

Let go of sleeve and ensure the pad is adequately compressed against the arch of the
foot.

4.1. Carefully slide your hands out of the sleeve

4.2. Feel the pad to locate the arch support and ensure that it is correctly positioned
under your arch

4.3.Walk across the room to ensure the support sits comfortably, if it does not repeat
step 3.

Ethical Considerations of Device:

Obese children may break the device, which not follow the beneficence or justice of the
patient.

If the device breaks, it will not work which will be unfair to overweight individuals.

Unique foot anatomy (such as a protruding ankle) could prevent the device from being
applied.

This will infringe on their justice, as certain disabilities may prevent use of the device.

Neurodivergent children with sensory issues (such as children with autism) may find the
device severely uncomfortable and overstimulating.

This may cause discomfort, hence violating nonmaleficence, and may prevent the child
from using the device, hence violating justice.

Extremely busy parents may put the device on incorrectly, especially if the device is
overly complicated, and incorrect use of the device could potentially do more harm to the
patient, violating nonmaleficence.

3.3 CFR 820.30 (d) Design and Development Outputs
MATERIAL SELECTION

Bleached Muslin was selected to ensure the shape of the pattern accurately fit into
place.

HYBRID SUPPORT

Gel-adhesive sandwich construction: Soft gel for immediate comfort surrounded by
adhesive to encase and deform with the gel.

HUMAN FACTORS

Familiar design allows children to put on the insert themselves, as if it were a regular
sock.

ASSEMBLY OVERVIEW

• Sleeve: Breathable Muslin.

• Pocket: Reinforced internal stitching.

• Insert: Gel-Adhesive Combination.

• Strap: Elastic Band

PROTOTYPE JOURNEY

V1: PROOF OF CONCEPT

Cardboard and foam inserts in standard socks.

Lesson: Verified the lift required but failed on stability.

V2: FUNCTIONAL ALPHA

Gel pads in compression sleeves.

Lesson: Improved stability; identified the need for a dedicated pad pocket. Need to refine
insert topography.

*Note: Due to project timeline constraints, development concluded at V2. The planned
V3 (Final Beta - Custom-molded hybrid inserts with reinforced pouch) remains a future
milestone for subsequent validation.*

3.4 CFR 820.30 (e) Design and Development Review
Regulatory Strategy:

Device Classification

Since most predicate devices listed are Class I devices (due to their low risk factor), the
device we create will most likely also be a Class I device.

A simple, external orthopedic creates little to no harm on the patient since it simply
forces the patient’s foot to align itself properly.

However, since we are focusing on children for the design of this device, we will need to
put a larger emphasis on molding the proper arch into the patient’s foot.

This is because they are at an extremely formative time of development, and any
discrepancy in the device may cause more harm than good.

FDA Submission Pathway

Since this device is Class I, we will need to consider several general controls for the
device.

These include manufacturing devices in accordance with cGMP regulations, labeling
devices in accordance with applicable regulations, and submitting a premarket
notification 510(k).

The main action item from the FDA submission pathway will be the 510k.

To tackle this, we must have an in-depth understanding of predicate devices, so we can
argue that it is substantially equivalent to other devices on the market.

Furthermore, we will need to know the specifications of our device inside and out and be
able to justify any design decisions we made along the way.

Reimbursement Strategy and Relevant Codes

Q66.51: Congenital pes planus, right foot (Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
[CMS], 2026).

Q66.52: Congenital pes planus, left foot (CMS, 2026).

Clinical Interpretation: Applied when the pediatric flatfoot represents a failure to develop
a normal structural arch from birth, without an outside trauma history.

M21.41: Acquired flat foot, right foot (CMS, 2026).

M21.42: Acquired flat foot, left foot (CMS, 2026).

Clinical Interpretation: Applied if the arch collapse is secondary to an outside condition,
such as pediatric posterior tibial tendon dysfunction, physical trauma, or underlying
ligamentous laxity.

HCPCS Code L3040: Foot, arch support, removable, premolded, longitudinal, each
(CMS, 2026).

Application: Direct fit for off-the-shelf, prefabricated pediatric devices that offer fixed or
minor modular modification configurations.

HCPCS Code L3000: Foot, insert, removable, molded to patient model, "UCB" type,
Berkeley Shell, each (CMS, 2026).

Application: Reserved for custom-fabricated devices built from a unique physical cast or
3D digital scan of an individual patient's foot.

Payer Policies and Coverage Landscape

Traditional commercial insurance and Medicare frequently classify prefabricated
orthopedic inserts as "non-covered over-the-counter personal care items".

However, because this device targets young children with symptomatic deformities, the
primary billing pathway shifts to state-managed Medicaid programs under the federally
mandated Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic, and Treatment (EPSDT) benefit.

If a pediatric podiatrist or general practitioner explicitly documents a diagnosis of
symptomatic Q66.5- or M21.4- accompanied by structural pain or gait abnormalities,
state Medicaid protocols will reimburse for prefabricated or adjustable orthotics to avoid
long-term skeletal degradation and future liability.

FDA Guidance Documentation & Standards:

Voluntary Consensus Standards

ISO 10993-1:2018: Biological evaluation of medical devices — Part 1: Evaluation and
testing within a risk management process.

Relevance: Mandatory for skin-surface contact devices with prolonged wear cycles.
Materials must undergo screening for cytotoxicity, sensitization, and intracutaneous

4. Technical Memo: Suggestions for Future Project Team
To the future BME capstone/design team taking over the Pediatric Arch Support project:

We have successfully developed this device up through our V2 functional alpha iteration.
By utilizing gel pads within compression sleeves, we significantly improved structural
stability over our V1 cardboard proof-of-concept and successfully identified the need for
a dedicated pad pocket.

Because of the constraints of our timeline this semester, we unfortunately never made it
to V3 (the final beta stage, which would have consisted of custom-molded hybrid inserts
with a reinforced pouch). Therefore, V3 remains ready for your team to fabricate and put
through rigorous biomechanical validation.

As you pick up where we left off, please direct your attention to the following key
learnings and areas for future improvement:

1. Material Containment: During our impact testing (specifically Impact #3), we observed
that the adhesive may struggle to contain the gel under high, dynamic loading. You will
need to address this limitation, potentially by exploring a TPU printed encasement to
fully reinforce the gel casing.

2. The "Growing Child" Constraint: Balancing the need to scale with child growth against
maintaining support is fundamentally a material science problem. Our breathable muslin
was a great start for donning human factors, but sleeve tension and elasticity must be
perfectly balanced against tissue compression limits to avoid circulatory constriction. We
recommend looking into flexible elastic fabric integration.

3. Manufacturing Feasibility: To make this highly tailored yet scalable, we strongly
suggest exploring a 3D Scan-to-Print workflow for the custom inserts.

4. Clinical Validation: A necessary next step for the V3 prototype will be a longitudinal
gait analysis using actual pediatric subjects. You will need to prove the device actively
corrects the Resting Calcaneal Stance Position (RCSP) while mitigating muscle fatigue.

Best of luck moving this design into the beta phase.

Sincerely,

Thomas Barnett, Levi Willgruber, and Hamza Al Halabi (Group 11)
